title: David Ellison Plans to Merge HBO Max and Paramount+ in Bold Streaming Strategy, Report Says
body:
The media‑tech landscape may soon see two of its biggest streaming rivals merged into a single platform, after Skydance Media chief executive David Ellison announced that, in the long run, he intends to combine HBO Max with Paramount+. The proposal, unveiled at a press briefing on Tuesday, signals an ambitious bid to reshape the fragmented streaming market, but industry insiders warn that the technical, regulatory and branding hurdles involved could keep the plan in the realm of speculation for years to come.

Ellison, who has steered Skydance into a broader entertainment ecosystem through high‑profile deals with both Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount Global, said the integration would “create a more compelling, unified experience for subscribers” and “leverage the deep libraries and original content pipelines of both services.” He emphasized that the vision is a “long‑term” goal, acknowledging that building the necessary technology infrastructure will be a protracted effort. “We’re not talking about a quick flip‑over,” he told reporters. “It’s about constructing a robust, scalable stack that can handle the combined content catalog, user data, and personalized recommendations across two historically distinct ecosystems.”

The notion of a joint HBO Max‑Paramount+ service has been floated before, but Ellison’s comments mark the first public endorsement from a senior executive with direct stakes in both entities. While Warner Bros. Discovery’s chief content officer Casey Bloys has not publicly addressed the idea, insiders suggest that internal alignment may be lacking. “If the leadership on the Warner side isn’t on the same page, any merger‑like initiative will stall at the planning stage,” said a source familiar with the discussions. The source added that both companies are currently focused on optimizing their individual platforms, rolling out new pricing tiers, and negotiating content‑distribution agreements that could be jeopardized by a premature partnership.

From a market perspective, the consolidation could address the “subscription fatigue” that has plagued consumers as the number of streaming services balloons. Analysts estimate that U.S. households now subscribe to an average of four to five services, a figure that strains budgets and dilutes viewership. A combined HBO Max‑Paramount+ offering could potentially capture a larger share of the premium streaming segment, leveraging HBO’s prestige dramas and Paramount’s expansive film library. However, the merger would also raise antitrust concerns, especially given the recent scrutiny of large media conglomerates by U.S. regulators. A joint platform would likely be evaluated for its impact on competition, pricing power, and the bargaining position of independent content creators.

Technical integration presents perhaps the most formidable obstacle. Both services run on distinct content‑delivery networks, recommendation algorithms, and user‑account architectures. Merging them would require a unified backend capable of handling billions of data points, ensuring seamless playback across devices, and preserving existing subscriber data without service interruptions. “We’re looking at a multi‑year engineering roadmap, potentially involving new cloud partnerships and a re‑architected identity management system,” explained a senior Skydance technologist who asked to remain anonymous. The cost of such an undertaking could run into the hundreds of millions, a figure that would need justification to shareholders on both sides.

Despite the challenges, Ellison’s announcement underscores a broader industry trend toward strategic alliances and platform convergence. As the streaming wars mature, the emphasis is shifting from sheer subscriber counts to sustainable profitability and differentiated content experiences. If a combined HBO Max‑Paramount+ service materializes, it could set a precedent for future collaborations among legacy media houses seeking scale without full mergers.

Looking ahead, the next few months will likely reveal whether the concept moves beyond visionary rhetoric. Stakeholder alignment, regulatory clearance, and the successful execution of a complex technical integration will determine if the two streaming giants can truly become one. For now, the industry watches closely, aware that any step toward consolidation could reshape the competitive dynamics of digital entertainment for years to come.
